case_study_insert.main_stem: Saltmarsh Harbour Ferries (SHF) is a sole trader in the coastal passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 12. Founded in 2012 by Captain Owen Pryce, the business runs two vessels on 14-minute crossings between Saltmarsh quay and the island of St Bride, with an autocratic leadership style and a hands-on, close-knit team. SHF plans to invest $480,000 in a new 60-seat hybrid ferry, financed by the sale of the older vessel for $150,000 and a $330,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.40 a unit and a selling price of $16, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. SHF faces rising labour turnover, which reached 21% among seasonal deck crew last summer.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Advertisement Extract — Summer 2027 brochure: "Island in 14 minutes — $16 return, family tickets 25% off, now with hybrid-electric sailings." Below the advert: Market research (June 2026) of 420 passengers found 66% would pay up to $4 more for a guaranteed seat on summer weekends; 71% rate hybrid ferries important; average crossing time is 14 minutes; customer complaints average 1.9% of crossings; seasonal bookings rose 12% year-on-year; 4 of 12 deck crew need renewed first-aid certification (off-the-job training at the maritime college costs $320 per crew member; on-the-job training is difficult alongside the tight sailing schedule).

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Saltmarsh Harbour Ferries for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $11.63 to $12.35 per hour from April 2026, raising crew costs. (2) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, increasing repayments on variable-rate loans. (3) Marine diesel costs have risen 10.9% year-on-year, and domestic overnight-stay spending on St Bride grew 5.3%, with holiday inflation running at 6.8%.

questions.question_text: SHF plans to finance the new hybrid ferry with the $150,000 sale of the older vessel and a $330,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for SHF of using the sale of the older vessel instead of relying solely on the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Selling the older vessel raises $150,000 without any interest or repayment obligation, cutting the amount SHF must borrow from $480,000 to $330,000 and reducing the strain of loan repayments while fixed costs already stand at $216,000 a year. Lower borrowing also means interest payable — $34,000 in 2025 — will rise less when the 5.5% base rate feeds through, directly protecting Owen Pryce's profit.

Point 2: The older vessel is ageing and costly to maintain, so selling it removes rising repair bills and safety risk while funding the $480,000 hybrid replacement. Retaining full control matters to a sole trader: by using the sale proceeds, Owen Pryce avoids extra lender conditions on how the 60-seat hybrid is deployed, keeps fare-setting freedom at $16, and shows good asset management to any future lender assessing the loan application.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Saltmarsh Harbour Ferries and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: SHF is launching the new hybrid ferry service to St Bride. Consider local radio advertising, summer brochure leaflet drops, or social media fare-deal campaigns. Which should SHF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: A spot on the regional station would reach commuters and holidaymakers planning St Bride trips, building awareness of the hybrid ferry with 14-minute crossings and family tickets 25% off. Radio suits the drive-then-sail audience on Saltmarsh quay routes and is more affordable than national media for a 12-person business. However, listener attention is fragmented, recall of fare details is low without repetition, and coverage beyond the Saltmarsh catchment is weak — many island-bound visitors come from much further afield.

Summer brochure leaflet drops: Dropping the Summer 2027 brochure (already read by 420 surveyed passengers) through regional hotels, holiday parks and tourist information centres reaches high-intent travellers with full fare tables, the hybrid-electric message and the family discount. Print is trusted by older island visitors and cheap to produce; wastage occurs on households with no travel plans, and print cannot create urgency or capture last-minute bookings.

Social media fare-deal campaigns: Geo-targeted social posts offering weekend fare deals, hybrid-ferry features and guaranteed-seat upsells speak directly to the 66% willing to pay up to $4 more for a guaranteed seat and the 71% who rate hybrid ferries important. Deals can be switched on for peak weekends, tracked through booking codes, and shared by island community groups — ideal for a 12-person team with limited time, and measurable end-to-end. Risks are reliance on platform reach and weaker penetration of older, non-digital islanders.

Recommendation: SHF should choose social media fare-deal campaigns. They reach exactly the passengers its research identifies, deliver measurable bookings at the lowest cost, and suit the sole trader's limited hours; the guaranteed-seat and hybrid messages differentiate SHF from competing transport. Local radio is rejected as too broad and costly per actual booking for a single-route ferry; brochure drops are rejected as the lead channel because they lack urgency and tracking, though a small print run in hotels should remain to reach older visitors; social campaigns should run continuously through the season.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SHF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SHF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why local radio and brochure drops are rejected as lead channels.

questions.question_text: SHF's seasonal deck crew labour turnover reached 21% last summer. Explain two benefits for SHF of using job enrichment to reduce this labour turnover.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives deck crew upgraded responsibilities — cross-training as mates, running passenger safety briefings and overseeing hybrid charging checks — making the role more varied and satisfying, which lifts esteem and reduces the boredom that drives summer deckhands to quit. With seasonal bookings up 12%, keeping trained crew able to supervise the new 60-seat hybrid protects service levels at peak.

Point 2: Enriched roles build loyalty and skill depth in a 12-person team, reducing recruitment and re-induction costs, since every departure forces Owen Pryce personally to recruit and brief replacements. Lower turnover also improves passenger safety and compliance — vital with 4 of 12 crew already needing first-aid renewal — and stabilises the 14-minute crossing schedule that anchors SHF's reputation and the 1.9% complaint rate.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SHF's turnover, schedule and safety.

questions.question_text: SHF needs to cover the summer peak on the new hybrid ferry. Consider hiring seasonal part-time deck crew or offering full-time permanent contracts to retain core staff. Which should SHF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Seasonal part-time contracts: Hiring part-time deck crew for June-to-September matches labour cost exactly to seasonal bookings, which rose 12% year-on-year, and lets SHF add capacity only when 420-passenger survey demand materialises. Payroll flexibility protects the tight margin on $16 fares and avoids employing crew in quiet January months. Drawbacks are higher turnover risk (already 21%), repeated training of temporary staff in hybrid-vessel safety routines, variable passenger experience, and the legal and morale burden of casual contracts among a close-knit 12-person team.

Full-time permanent contracts: Retaining core crew on permanent terms builds loyalty, deepens hybrid-vessel competence, and gives Owen Pryce a stable safety culture; permanent staff are more invested in passenger care, complaint reduction below 1.9% and reliable 14-minute crossings. The trade-off is a higher fixed wage bill year-round, harder to absorb in winter when volume drops, and the risk of carrying surplus labour if island tourism slows.

Decision: SHF should choose full-time permanent contracts for the essential core crew of deckhands and mates, supplemented by seasonal part-time staff only for the August peak weeks. Permanent core staff protect safety, service quality and the hybrid launch, directly attacking the 21% turnover; seasonal top-ups add flexible capacity for the 12% booking surge. Seasonal-only recruitment is rejected as a sole strategy — it would entrench turnover, multiply first-aid and hybrid training costs ($320 per crew member) and weaken passenger confidence — while permanent contracts for every role regardless of winter demand would breach fixed costs of $216,000 and strain the $330,000 bank loan before the hybrid generates full revenue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two contract options with limited application to SHF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of SHF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of SHF with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety, turnover and seasonality.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SHF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($16 − $6.40) = $216,000 ÷ $9.60 = 22,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 22,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16 − $6.40 = $9.60. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SHF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Owen Pryce can compare the 22,500-unit break-even output with production of 45,000 crossings to confirm the service is profitable, with a margin of safety of 22,500 units, informing whether the hybrid ferry can be sold as a family-fare product without losses.
2. Contribution per unit of $9.60 lets SHF model the $4 guaranteed-seat premium: guaranteed summer-weekend seats would earn $13.60 contribution, so managers can forecast how many premium seats per sailing pay back the reservation system needed for that promise.
3. Contribution data lets Owen Pryce check the expansion is bankable: the hybrid ferry must cover its share of fixed costs of $216,000 and the $330,000 bank loan, so crossing volumes and fare promotions can be tied to the repayment schedule.
4. Unit cost data ($216,000 ÷ 45,000 units + $6.40 = $11.20 a unit) helps benchmark crossing economics, target the 1.9% complaint rate and 21% turnover that inflate crewing costs, and renegotiate marine diesel and maintenance contracts as diesel prices rise 10.9%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 22,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.60 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 22,500 units vs 45,000-unit output; guaranteed-seat premium modelling; loan-repayment feasibility for the $480,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.20 to tackle turnover and diesel costs.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SHF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has SHF's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 42.5%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 figures ($'000): gross profit $255,000 ÷ revenue $600,000 × 100 = 42.5%; 2025: gross profit $324,000 ÷ revenue $720,000 × 100 = 45.0%. Operating profit against revenue: 2024: $60,000 ÷ $600,000 × 100 = 10.0%; 2025: $108,000 ÷ $720,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit against capital employed: 2024: $60,000 ÷ $500,000 × 100 = 12.0%; 2025: $108,000 ÷ $720,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Cost of sales grew from $345,000 to $396,000 as crossings approached 45,000, but fell from 57.5% to 55.0% of revenue, and capital employed rose from $500,000 to $720,000 as the older vessel sale and hybrid investment flowed through the accounts; interest payable rose from $28,000 to $34,000.

Evaluation: Profitability has strengthened on every measure. Revenue grew 20.0% from $600,000 to $720,000, in step with 45,000 units and a 12% rise in seasonal bookings. Gross profit improved from 42.5% to 45.0%, reflecting solid control of the $6.40 variable cost despite marine diesel inflation of 10.9%. Operating profit improved sharply from 10.0% to 15.0%, showing overheads and crewing were managed well even with interest payable up from $28,000 to $34,000. Operating profit against capital employed improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, so the enlarged asset base — now including the hybrid investment — is generating a better return. Caution: as a sole trader, Owen Pryce bears all residual risk; capital employed grew 44.0%, so the improvement depends on sustaining summer volumes and converting the guaranteed-seat premium into cash. Fuel volatility and wage rises to $12.35 per hour could compress these gains quickly if fares stay at $16.

Conclusion: SHF's financial performance has improved. Gross profit (42.5% to 45.0%), operating profit against revenue (10.0% to 15.0%) and operating profit against capital employed (12.0% to 15.0%) all rose, supported by 20.0% revenue growth. Owen Pryce should protect these gains with early diesel hedging, off-season cost discipline and continued hybrid-driven marketing before the fixed-cost load of the expansion fully bites.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether SHF's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SHF of operating the new 60-seat hybrid ferry.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The hybrid ferry cuts fuel burn and emissions on the 14-minute Saltmarsh–St Bride crossing, appealing to the 71% of surveyed passengers who rate hybrid ferries important and reinforcing the 66% who would pay $4 more for a guaranteed seat. Lower marine diesel consumption directly offsets the 10.9% year-on-year diesel price rise and supports SHF's family-ticket 25% off positioning, helping win listings in island tourism marketing and filling the larger 60-seat capacity profitably at $16 per crossing.

Disadvantage: A 60-seat vessel costs far more to run than SHF's current boats: the $480,000 purchase consumes the $150,000 vessel sale and adds a $330,000 bank loan, raising fixed costs and interest payable above the $34,000 recorded for 2025. Hybrid drivetrains also require specialist maintenance and charging infrastructure at Saltmarsh quay that the 12-person crew may not hold, and any technical teething problems would ground the core service during peak summer weeks when seasonal bookings are up 12%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SHF's fleet, finances and customers.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $12.35, the interest rate rise to 5.5% and the 10.9% rise in marine diesel costs will affect SHF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $12.35 per hour): With a workforce of 12, mainly deck crew and kiosk staff, a 6.2% rise adds roughly $1,500 per employee a year, or about $18,000 across the team — a noticeable but survivable increase, and one that reinforces the value of Owen Pryce's job-enrichment and retention drive against the 21% seasonal turnover problem. Productivity gains (45,000 units ÷ 12 staff ≈ 3,750 units per person) can absorb much of the uplift.

Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): SHF's $330,000 bank loan becomes costlier by roughly $2,475 a year per 0.75 percentage points, nudging interest payable beyond the $34,000 in Appendix 2 — the mildest direct cash impact of the three, and manageable for a sole trader that can fix its rate or shorten the term using strong summer cash flows. Higher rates may also cool unsecured borrowing for small tourism businesses on St Bride, reducing competitor capacity.

Marine diesel cost rise (10.9%): Diesel dominates variable costs inside the $6.40 a unit figure. A 10.9% rise adds roughly $0.40–$0.55 per unit; across 45,000 crossings a year that is $18,000–$25,000 a year, dragging contribution from $9.60 toward $9.05–$9.20 and squeezing exactly the margin that must service the $330,000 loan and justify the $480,000 hybrid. The new hybrid ferry mitigates this partially through lower fuel burn, but diesel still prices every crossing.

Conclusion: The 10.9% rise in marine diesel costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 45,000 annual crossings, totalling roughly $18,000–$25,000 a year, and strikes the cost line most resistant to improvement now that wage and loan effects are comparatively small. The minimum wage rise adds around $18,000 and the interest rate rise only a few thousand dollars; SHF should accelerate the hybrid's efficiency benefits, negotiate bulk marine-fuel contracts, review the $16 fare and protect the $4 guaranteed-seat premium to defend margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SHF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SHF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SHF with a well-justified judgment that the diesel cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
